evidence.title: Uncertainty when health advice conflicts
evidence.summary: US adults reported at least some difficulty deciding which information to trust when they encountered conflicting health advice.
evidence.sample: 5,111 US adults in Pew Research Center’s American Trends Panel; weighted to represent the US adult population.
evidence.source_title: Where Do Americans Get Health Information, and What Do They Trust?
limitations: This measures reported difficulty, including ‘somewhat difficult’; it is not a test of whether respondents correctly identified misinformation.
The finding describes US adults and is not an estimate for India. Publication in 2026 follows survey fieldwork in 2025.

evidence.title: Medical claims with very low or no supporting evidence
evidence.summary: Researchers assigned their lowest evidence grade to 193 of 309 assessed claims in a selected sample of health professional videos about cancer and diabetes.
evidence.scope: Selected YouTube videos · cancer and diabetes
evidence.fieldwork: Video search and data capture: 20 to 21 June 2025
evidence.sample: 309 eligible videos, each with at least 10,000 views and a specific health claim; searches used Korean terms, with Korean  and English language videos eligible.
evidence.source_title: The Quality of Evidence of and Engagement With Video Medical Claims
limitations: This selected sample does not represent all online medical content, all specialties or all countries.
A low evidence grade does not by itself establish that a claim is false or that it caused patient harm.

evidence.title: Doctors stepping in after online misinformation
evidence.summary: Surveyed Canadian physicians reported having to step in after patients acted on inaccurate online health advice, either to avert harm or manage its effects. The question included AI advice.
evidence.sample: 645 practising physicians in Canada, recruited through Canadian Medical Association outreach; results were weighted by region of practice.
evidence.source_title: Disconnected health systems and misinformation are putting patient care at risk, say Canadian physicians
limitations: This is physicians’ reported experience, not an audited count of injuries or an estimate of how many patients were harmed.
This reports experience of intervention, not the share of appointments or patients affected. The sample is Canadian.

evidence.title: Limited confidence in judging AI health information
evidence.summary: US adults said they were not confident they could distinguish true from false health information supplied by AI tools or chatbots.
evidence.sample: 2,480 US adults surveyed online and by telephone in English and Spanish; overall sampling margin of error ±3 percentage points.
evidence.source_title: KFF Tracking Poll on Health Information and Trust: Use of Social Media and AI For Health Information and Advice
limitations: The percentage combines ‘not too’ and ‘not at all’ confident. It measures confidence, not demonstrated accuracy or actual exposure to harmful advice.
This US survey does not establish a prevalence rate for India.

evidence.title: AI is already part of health information seeking
evidence.summary: US adults reported having used chatbots for at least one of eight health purposes, such as understanding symptoms, treatments, diagnoses or lab results.
evidence.sample: 3,488 US adults surveyed by Pew Research Center; the measure covers ever using AI for at least one of eight listed health or medical reasons.
evidence.source_title: From Diagnoses to Treatments, Why Americans Use AI Chatbots for Health
limitations: This is an ‘ever used’ measure, not monthly or daily usage. It should not be compared directly with surveys using a different time window.
Adoption and perceived helpfulness do not establish medical accuracy, patient harm or benefit. The population is US adults.

evidence.title: Uncertainty about health information in Indian schools
evidence.summary: In a five city school study, 1,129 of 2,331 students were unsure whether health information shared on social media was accurate and reliable.
evidence.sample: 2,331 students in grades 9 to 12 across 75 schools in Ahmedabad, Lucknow, Guwahati, Bhubaneswar and Visakhapatnam. Table 5 reports 1,129 unsure responses.
evidence.source_title: Social Media Literacy and Health Information Seeking Behavior Among School Students and Educators in India: A Needs Assessment Under Project Info Suraksha
limitations: The article was published in October 2026, but the data were collected in 2023.
Selected schools in five cities do not constitute a nationally representative sample of Indian adults or patients. The finding measures students’ perceptions.

evidence.title: Choosing the next step requires more than model knowledge
evidence.summary: In a randomized UK study, participants using three LLMs did no better than the control group at selecting the appropriate next action in simulated medical scenarios.
evidence.sample: 1,298 adults contributed 2,400 interactions across ten scenarios. The study compared GPT 4o, Llama 3 and Command R+ with participants’ usual resources.
evidence.source_title: Reliability of LLMs as medical assistants for the general public: a randomized preregistered study
limitations: The next step comparison found no statistically significant difference; identifying relevant conditions was a separate outcome.
The study used 2024 models and simulated scenarios. It did not assess current models, real patient outcomes or DigiDr.

further_reading.title: What changes when health AI has to remain useful over time?
A human in the loop is not automatically meaningful oversight
Medical models can look healthy while targeted knowledge becomes unsafe
Health AI needs realistic, expert reviewed evaluation
